Short answer: on these facts he has a credible seaman-status argument, and I'd expect him to clear the test more often than not. The reassignment to the dock is the best defense angle, but it's a fact fight.

**The test.** Under *Chandris v. Latsis*, a Jones Act seaman must (1) have duties that contribute to the function of a vessel or the accomplishment of its mission, and (2) have a connection to a vessel (or identifiable fleet) in navigation that is substantial in both duration and nature.

**Prong one** is a low bar. Processing fish aboard a catcher-processor contributes to the vessel's mission; the factory line *is* the mission. I wouldn't contest it for his time aboard.

**Prong two, duration.** *Chandris* adopts a rule of thumb: a worker who spends less than about 30% of his time in the service of a vessel in navigation generally shouldn't qualify. Looking at his employment as a whole:

- Employed Jan 18 – Jun 28: about 162 days.
- Aboard: Jan 18 – Apr 11 (~84 days) plus the May gear run (~4) = ~88 days.
- That's roughly 54%, comfortably over 30%.

**Prong two, nature.** *Harbor Tug & Barge Co. v. Papai* asks whether the worker's duties take him to sea and expose him to its perils, rather than being essentially land-based. Three months on a factory trawler in the Bering Sea during A-season is about as sea-based as it gets.

**The reassignment.** *Chandris* recognizes that when a worker's essential duties change, for example a seaman reassigned to a land-based job, the analysis can follow the new assignment. That's our best argument: at the moment of injury he was dock crew, on the dock, doing longshore-type work. But courts are wary of letting an employer defeat status by moving someone ashore between seasons, and ten weeks on the dock after a full season aboard could be framed as a temporary shore stint. It will turn on whether the move was a real change in his job or a gap-filler until the next trip.

**If he's not a seaman,** his remedy for a dock injury while handling cargo is likely the LHWCA (and possibly Alaska workers' comp), which is a much better outcome for the client.

**Gut check for the partner:** likely a seaman on the whole-employment numbers. The reassignment is a legitimate argument worth developing in discovery (the paperwork moving him to the dock, whether he was slated for B-season, who was paying him), but I wouldn't promise it.

Short version for the client: keep paying, adjust the rate on evidence, don't sit on the surgery request, and run down the prior-surgery issue now, because it may end the maintenance and cure claim entirely.

**The obligation.** Maintenance and cure is owed to a seaman injured in the service of the vessel, regardless of fault. Maintenance is a daily living stipend (food and lodging comparable to what he had aboard); cure is reasonable medical care. Both run until maximum medical improvement. Hurting his back pulling pots mid-season is squarely within it.

**The punitive threat is real.** Under *Atlantic Sounding Co. v. Townsend*, a willful or callous failure to pay maintenance and cure can support punitive damages and attorney's fees. The letter is building that record. Whatever we do has to look like a reasoned, prompt response, not a stall.

**The rate.** $85/day is a demand. Maintenance should track his reasonable actual costs of food and lodging. $30/day is low for the Seattle area unless he's living with family rent-free. Ask counsel for documentation (lease, utilities, food), and if it supports a higher number, raise the rate going forward. Courts are far less sympathetic to an employer that never asked than to one that asked and adjusted.

**The surgery request.** Cure covers surgery reasonably necessary to reach maximum medical improvement. Respond promptly: request the treating surgeon's records and schedule an independent medical exam before approving, and put a date on it. A short, documented review is defensible. An open-ended hold on surgery is how punitive damages claims get made.

**The prior surgery: this is the *McCorpen* defense.** Under *McCorpen v. Central Gulf Steamship Corp.*, an employer can deny maintenance and cure if (1) the seaman intentionally misrepresented or concealed medical facts, (2) the concealed facts were material to the decision to hire him, and (3) there's a connection between the concealed condition and the injury now claimed. A prior back surgery left off a pre-employment medical form is the classic set-up.

exchanges.user: Partner read the draft Harlan memo and wants me to walk through the primary duty rule section at the 2:00 case meeting. exchanges.assistant:
Both good questions, and the second is the one the partner will push on.

**It isn't a captain-only rule.** It grew out of cases about masters and officers, which is why it's associated with captains, but the principle is about the duty, not the rank. The classic formulation, from the Second Circuit in *Walker v. Lykes Bros.*, is that a seaman can't recover from his employer for an injury caused by his own failure to perform a duty he consciously assumed as a term of his employment. A chief engineer specifically responsible for maintaining deck machinery fits that as well as a master does. The question is whether the task that went wrong was *his* job, not whether he commanded the vessel.

**How it differs from comparative fault.** This is the heart of it:

- Comparative fault *reduces* damages. If the jury finds Kiska 60% at fault and Harlan 40%, he recovers 60%. Under the Jones Act, even substantial fault by the seaman doesn't bar recovery.
- The primary duty rule is a complete *bar*. The logic is that when the employer's only breach is the seaman's own failure to do his job, there's no separate employer negligence to compare. Holding the employer liable would effectively pay the seaman for his own breach of the employment contract.

So the rule matters because it turns "reduced recovery" into "no recovery."

**The limits, and why I overstated it in the memo.** Courts, including in the Ninth Circuit, apply the rule narrowly. It generally doesn't apply where:

1. the injury came from a condition the seaman didn't create and wasn't in a position to correct,
2. the seaman was following an order, or
3. the employer failed to give him the means to perform the duty.

Number 3 is our problem. Harlan logged the weeping fitting and emailed the port engineer for replacement hoses the next day, and the parts were "on order" for eleven days. Plaintiff will say he did exactly what his duty required and the failure was Kiska's shoreside supply chain. On those facts a court is unlikely to let the rule bar the claim, and it has little force against unseaworthiness, which doesn't turn on fault at all.

**For the meeting:** present primary duty as a secondary argument that probably won't survive the Aug 4 email, and put the weight on comparative fault: he knew the hose was weeping, marked it "monitor," and didn't tag the crane out while waiting for parts. That's a real reduction argument, and the reserve should rest on it rather than on a complete bar.

I'd advise against removing. Here's the reasoning.

**Jones Act claims aren't removable.** The Jones Act incorporates FELA, and 28 U.S.C. § 1445(a) bars removal of FELA actions filed in state court. A properly pleaded Jones Act claim stays where the plaintiff filed it. The saving-to-suitors clause also lets him bring his general maritime claims (unseaworthiness, maintenance and cure) in state court, and courts are divided on whether those can be removed on admiralty jurisdiction alone. Even where they can, they'd usually be remanded alongside a non-removable Jones Act claim.

**The exception: a fraudulently pleaded Jones Act claim.** A defendant can remove if it shows the Jones Act claim is baseless, meaning the plaintiff has no reasonable possibility of establishing seaman status. The court may look past the pleadings, but it resolves disputed facts and ambiguities in the plaintiff's favor. That's a very high bar.

We don't meet it on what we have. He spent the whole A-season, about three months, on the factory line of a catcher-processor in the Bering Sea. Whether the dock reassignment changed his status is exactly the kind of disputed fact a court resolves for the plaintiff at the removal stage. Expect a remand, and possibly a fee award under § 1447(c) if the court finds removal objectively unreasonable.

**What we give up by staying in King County is less than it looks.**
- The state court applies federal maritime law substantively, *Chandris* included.
- A Jones Act plaintiff gets a jury in either forum.
- We can move for summary judgment on seaman status under CR 56. If we win, the Jones Act and unseaworthiness claims fall away and what's left is a much smaller case.

**Timing:** if the client wants to try removal anyway, the 30-day clock runs from service, not filing. Confirm the service date.

**Recommendation:** answer in King County, get the payroll records, dock timesheets, and crew lists early, and build toward a seaman-status summary judgment motion. That's a better use of the fight than a removal we're likely to lose.

It feels like the lie should be the whole point, but it isn't, and seeing why tells you how to win this.

**What *McCorpen* is for.** Maintenance and cure is a no-fault obligation, historically justified by treating seamen as wards of admiralty. *McCorpen* isn't a penalty for dishonesty. It's a narrow exception: the employer shouldn't bear the cost of a medical risk it would have declined if the seaman had told the truth. That's why the defense has three elements, not one:

1. **Intentional concealment.** The seaman knowingly withheld or misrepresented medical facts. This doesn't require proof he meant to defraud anyone; a knowing "no" to a clear, direct question usually does it. Question 14 is about as direct as it gets.
2. **Materiality.** The concealed facts would have mattered to the hiring decision. A question on the employer's own form is strong evidence of that, and the port captain can confirm the Aleutian Star wouldn't have put a post-discectomy deckhand on a crab boat without clearance.
3. **Connection.** The concealed condition is causally linked to the injury now claimed.

The lie gets you element one. Element three is what ties the lie to *this* claim. If he'd hidden a prior knee surgery and then hurt his back, the lie would be just as real, but the employer would be escaping liability for a risk that had nothing to do with it. The connection element prevents that.

**So does L3-L4 vs. L4-L5 break the connection?** Probably not, if we build the record. Courts applying *McCorpen* generally don't require the identical injury; they ask whether the new injury is to the same body part or region and related to the prior condition. Adjacent-segment degeneration after lumbar surgery is a recognized phenomenon: altering one level can increase the load on its neighbors. If Dr. Hsu can say, to a reasonable degree of medical probability, that the 2021 L4-L5 surgery made the L3-L4 level more vulnerable, element three is met. Without that testimony, the "different level" argument has real traction.

**Two reminders:**
- *McCorpen* only defeats maintenance and cure. It doesn't bar his Jones Act or unseaworthiness claims, though the prior surgery still matters to causation and damages there.
- Keep paying under reservation until we have a ruling, or at least Dr. Hsu's opinion in hand.

**Next step:** ask Dr. Hsu to review the 2021 operative report and the 2026 MRI and give us a declaration focused specifically on the adjacent-segment link.

Defendant does not dispute that Plaintiff was a seaman during the 2026 A-season, when he worked on the processing line aboard the F/T Northern Resolve. The question is whether he was still one eleven weeks after the company reassigned him to its dock crew in Unalaska. He was not.

**1. Under *Chandris*, a change in essential duties resets the analysis.**

Seaman status requires a connection to a vessel in navigation that is substantial in both duration and nature. *Chandris, Inc. v. Latsis*. The inquiry looks at the worker's overall employment, but not indefinitely backward: the Supreme Court recognized that when a maritime worker's basic assignment changes, his seaman status may change as well, and the analysis is then measured by the new assignment. A seaman reassigned to a land-based job does not carry his former status ashore with him.

Plaintiff's assignment changed on April 14, 2026. The company's letter of that date assigned him to "dock crew until further notice." (Ex. __.) His payroll moved to Resolve Seafoods Shoreside LLC the same day. (Ex. __.) For the next seventy-two days he worked on the Unalaska dock under a shoreside supervisor, loading and unloading product and mending nets. (Timesheets, Ex. __; [Supervisor] Decl. ¶¶ __.) When the Northern Resolve's B-season crew list was finalized in early June, he was not on it. (Ex. __.) This was not a gap between trips. It was a new job.

**2. Measured from April 14, Plaintiff fails the duration element.**

From April 14 through his June 28 injury, Plaintiff spent four of seventy-six days aboard a vessel: the May 19–22 gear run to Akutan. (Timesheets, Ex. __; Crew List, Ex. __.) That is about five percent of his time, far below the thirty-percent guideline *Chandris* adopted for a substantial connection.

**3. The nature element fails independently.**

*Harbor Tug & Barge Co. v. Papai* asks whether a worker's duties take him to sea and regularly expose him to its perils, as opposed to being essentially land-based. His duties after April 14 were performed on a dock. The single gear run was a discrete, four-day errand, not a regular feature of his work, and it does not convert a land-based job into a sea-based one.[^1]

Because Plaintiff's connection to the Northern Resolve after April 14 was insubstantial in both duration and nature, he was not a seaman when he was injured, and his Jones Act and unseaworthiness claims fail as a matter of law.

[^1]: Plaintiff is not without a remedy. An employee injured on a dock while handling product for shipment may be covered by the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, 33 U.S.C. § 901 et seq., and may also have a claim under Alaska's workers' compensation statute. Defendant takes no position here on which applies; the point is only that the Jones Act does not.
